items.snippet: M&A have frustratingly failed to realize deal value consistently due to people a...
items.raw_snippet: M&A have frustratingly failed to realize deal value consistently due to people and cultural integration challenges, a problem exacerbated by lack of quantifiable data. However, a new era of AI-powered platforms is transforming M&A due diligence by making leadership and cultural compatibility measurable pre-deal. According to KPMG’s 2026 M&A Deal Market Study, both groups identified integration due diligence as the critical focus for ensuring value realization. Research spanning three decades, from Cartwright and Cooper’s 1993 work in the Academy of Management Perspectives on organizational incompatibility, to Harding and Rouse’s 2007 HBR article on 'Human Due Diligence,’ to McKinsey’s 2023 study on programmatic acquirers, the research consistently shows that when the people aspect of M&A is ignored or overlooked, this contributes to deal value not being realized. According to the founders of three AI-powered platforms, Humanaq (powered by MiliMatch), Grodivo, and NayaDaya, these companies are making culture and leadership compatibility measurable before day one.

items.snippet: # An Acquisition by Another Name: Reverse Acquihires Under the Clayton Act. Incr...
items.raw_snippet: # An Acquisition by Another Name: Reverse Acquihires Under the Clayton Act. Increasingly, companies competing in the artificial-intelligence (AI) industry engage in “reverse acquihires” to hire key AI personnel from startups without formally acquiring the startup. In a reverse acquihire, the two firms do not merge, nor does one firm formally acquire the other. As a result, some have assumed that reverse acquihires are not subject to Section 7 of the Clayton Act, the principal antitrust statute governing mergers. In a reverse acquihire, Firm *A*—the reverse-acquihiring firm—agrees with Firm *B*—the reverse-acquihired firm—to hire some, but not all, of Firm *B*’s leadership and/or AI researchers or engineers. While antitrust regulators and members of Congress have noticed and begun investigating reverse acquihires in AI,6 a crucial question remains: are reverse acquihires in AI, or other industries, subject to Section 7 of the Clayton Act—the primary antitrust law on mergers and acquisitions—even though no formal merger or acquisition occurs?

Opened in July 2025, the Center for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Data Science of the Paris Brain Institute federates unique multidisciplinary expertise to advance brain understanding and improve brain health. It is housed in a dedicated facility located a 5-minute walk from the main building. ## What is the Center for AI and Data Science? The Center aims at being an international hub in AI and data science for neuroscience, resulting in disruptive methodological advances and in major breakthroughs in understanding, preventing and treating brain disorders. Building on the Institute’s unique multidisciplinary environment - bringing together medicine, neurobiology, mathematics, and computer science - the Center leverages exceptionally rich research and clinical data, supported by state-of-the-art core facilities and a unique medical ecosystem. Its ambition is to open a novel era in neuroscience and brain health, resulting in more accurate diagnosis, accelerating therapeutic discovery, and advancing precision medicine. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly an operational reality in the field of counter-terrorism. To examine how AI continues to reshape counter-terrorism institutions, decision making, and operational, including with regard to its responsible use, this CT Week side event will explore and identify strategic priorities for Member States in adapting counter-terrorism policies and cooperation frameworks to the opportunities and risks posed by artificial intelligence. The event, organized by the European Union, India, Japan and the United Arab Emirates in cooperation with UNOCT and UNICRI, will foster a shared understanding of the strategic implications of AI for counter-terrorism and will serve as a basis for continued engagement with partners under a broader strategic framework. items.snippet: # Disappointed with AI, Ford moves to re-hire 350 former workers. ## The automak...
items.raw_snippet: # Disappointed with AI, Ford moves to re-hire 350 former workers. ## The automaker tried the technology for automated quality control, but it was unable to detect enough problems. Ford has rehired approximately 350 experienced engineers after the company’s investment in AI and automated quality control systems failed to meet expectations, according to Bloomberg. In short, the technology did not detect enough problems. “We mistakenly believed that we could create a high-quality product simply by introducing artificial intelligence and inputting our design requirements,” Charles Poon, head of Ford’s hardware development, told Bloomberg. The rehired quality inspectors — known internally as “gray beard” engineers for their experience and years with the company — are now working to identify defects before components reach the factories. Still, Ford is not abandoning AI completely; the experienced engineers will be asked to help train younger employees and improve the company’s AI tools. ### EU: Microsoft, Amazon cloud services could be classified as gatekeepers.

The **Distinguished Engineer – AI Adoption** will be responsible for accelerating enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence by evaluating emerging AI technologies, designing reusable frameworks, developing prototypes, and enabling business units to safely and effectively apply AI to high-value use cases. This role will serve as a hands-on technical leader across enterprise AI initiatives, working with internal teams and external AI vendors to assess capabilities, test solutions, define decision frameworks, and establish repeatable engineering patterns. The Distinguished AI Adoption Engineer will help business units identify, prototype, and scale AI solutions using the right combination of models, platforms, tools, and architectures. •    Evaluate AI vendors, platforms, foundation models, agentic tools, orchestration frameworks, and emerging AI capabilities through hands-on testing, proof of concepts, benchmarks, and technical assessments.
